title: SafetyClearance
description:
The manifest that must exist, verify, and be COMPLETE before anything leaves the device or reaches a printer. Designed by Codex on issue #21; this is the contract form of it.

WHY A MANIFEST AND NOT A FIELD ON EACH RECORD

A per-record `is_safe` flag is checked at some point and acted on at another, and the gap between them is where the failure lives: the selection changes, a photo is swapped in, and the check that passed was about a different set. So clearance is bound to an EXACT publication -- this sink, these media ids, in this order, under this classifier and this config digest -- and hashed. The renderer or service verifies the hash against the inputs it is ACTUALLY about to publish, inside the same operation that creates the export. There is no window in which the checked set and the published set can differ.

THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST

Absence is `indeterminate`, and indeterminate BLOCKS. A missing verdict, an unloadable classifier, a config digest mismatch, an inference timeout, a stale verdict for a proxy that has since changed, a row that simply is not there -- all of them are indeterminate. Only `cleared` proceeds.

This is the opposite of how safety checks usually fail. The common shape is a check that silently no-ops when its model is missing, so everything downstream reads the absence as a pass. This project has already shipped one gate with exactly that defect (a model load gate that permitted weights whose hash had never been computed), and the fix cost more than building it correctly would have.

WHAT MAY AND MAY NOT BE OVERRIDDEN

A POSITIVE classifier result may be overridden per item by a human: a parent may decide a breastfeeding photo belongs in the family album, and the classifier does not get a veto over that. The override is recorded in the manifest with who and when, so the decision is attributable.

A MISSING result may NOT be overridden -- not by a flag, not by a default, not by a global bypass, not by an empty override list. 'Nobody checked' and 'somebody checked and disagreed' are different states, and only the second is a decision.

manifest_id.description:
BLAKE3 over the manifest body: this document with `manifest_id` and `decision` removed, serialised by the RFC 8785 rule this repository already uses for `edl_id`, `job_id` and `params_digest` -- keys sorted by code unit, `,` and `:` separators, no whitespace, UTF-8, and every number rendered by ECMAScript `Number::toString` with exponent notation REFUSED rather than written.

THE ALGORITHM CHANGED IN #21 AND THE OLD ONE WAS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE. It said 'the SERIALISED BYTES of this document with manifest_id and decision removed. Bytes rather than a re-serialisation.' There are no such bytes: you cannot delete two keys from a byte string without re-serialising it, so every implementation would have invented its own canonical form -- which is the exact divergence the sentence was trying to prevent. models/policy/digest.py can hash bytes because a config file IS the artifact; a manifest body is a projection of one, so it has to be constructed.

The number rule is the load-bearing half. Python writes the float 1.0 as `1.0` where JavaScript writes `1`, and a manifest that verifies in the pipeline and fails in the renderer is a gate that blocks correct output, which is how gates get disabled. `contracts/vectors/safety-clearance-manifest-id.json` pins the exact pre-image bytes, and both the Python and TypeScript implementations are checked against it -- a digest mismatch says only that something diverged, the pre-image says which field did.

WHAT EXCLUDING `decision` MEANS, STATED SO NOBODY HAS TO REDISCOVER IT. Two manifests that differ ONLY in their decision block hash to the SAME manifest_id -- they describe the same publication, and the decision is a derived assertion about it rather than part of it. That is safe exactly as long as every verifier RECOMPUTES the decision from `items` and denies on disagreement, which is what `ClearanceDecision` already requires and what both implementations do. It is not safe if any consumer ever reads `cleared_for_publication` and believes it. The vectors file carries this pair as `same-body-different-decision` so the property is tested rather than assumed.

manifest_version.description: Format version of the manifest itself. A verifier that does not recognise this value MUST DENY rather than attempt a best-effort parse. Deny-by-default on an unknown version is what stops an old renderer from ignoring a field a newer planner added -- and the field it ignores will be the one that was added because something went wrong.

sink.description: Where this publication is going. Clearance is NOT transferable between sinks: a photo cleared for a private printed book has not thereby been cleared for a public share link, and the thresholds differ. A verifier must check that the sink it is serving matches this value exactly.

sink_detail.description: Free text naming the specific destination (vendor, recipient scope, model provider) for the audit trail. NEVER parsed, never used to make a decision -- a decision that depends on a free-text field is a decision an attacker can influence.

items.description: One entry per media id in the publication, in PUBLICATION ORDER. Order is part of the identity: a manifest whose items match by set but not by order describes a different publication, and a verifier comparing sets rather than sequences would accept a reordered book.

ClassifierPin.title: ClassifierPin
ClassifierPin.description: Which model produced these verdicts. A verdict from a model you cannot identify is not evidence, and a verdict produced under a different config is a verdict about a different decision boundary -- score_threshold 0.3 and 0.5 are different classifiers to every consumer.

class_order.description:
WHICH COLUMN OF THE CLASSIFIER'S OUTPUT VECTOR IS WHICH CLASS, as the producer applied it.

The head emits an unlabelled `[-1, 3]` tensor. `ClassScores` is keyed by name, so by the time scores reach this manifest the mapping has already been applied and is no longer visible -- and if it was applied wrongly, nothing here or downstream can tell. Transpose two columns and every breastfeeding photograph classifies as `explicit`, every score is in range, every count adds up, the manifest validates, and no test fails. That is the whole reason this field exists: it is the only place the mapping is written down where a machine can check it.

It is a `const`, so the only valid value is the contract's own order and a transposed manifest is REJECTED BY VALIDATION rather than by review. Const does not make it pointless to write: the producer must copy it out of the config that governed the run, and `models/schema/model-config.schema.json` pins the same three strings in the same order on the safety classifier's output. A config whose `class_order` was edited can no longer produce a manifest that validates.

Order, not a set. `["suggestive", "explicit", "medical_or_artistic"]` contains the same three strings and describes a different model.

load_mode.description: Which gate the host was running under. A verdict produced by a DEVELOPMENT-mode host -- unpinned weights, unverified licence -- must never clear a real publication, and a verifier serving a release sink must refuse it. Recorded rather than assumed, because 'we were only testing' is how unverified weights reach production.

Thresholds.title: Thresholds
Thresholds.description:
The decision boundaries actually applied, per class. Recorded rather than referenced because the config can change underneath a stored verdict, and a verdict whose threshold you cannot reconstruct cannot be re-audited.

The classes are separate on purpose. Collapsing them into one 'nsfw' bit produces the two classic failures: a breastfeeding photo or a post-surgery record treated as pornography, and a bikini holiday photo treated as safe for a public share. A family library contains all three, and the right handling differs for each.

ItemVerdict.title: ItemVerdict
ItemVerdict.description: One media id's clearance, bound to the exact bytes that were classified.

evidence_id.description: The PROXY the classifier actually saw. Not the media id: a proxy can be regenerated -- a better decoder, a corrected orientation, a different size -- and a verdict about the old proxy is not evidence about the new one. A verifier must confirm this matches the proxy the publication is built from, or treat the verdict as stale, which is indeterminate, which blocks.

verdict.description:
`cleared` is the ONLY value that permits automatic publication.

`blocked` means the classifier scored above a threshold. It may be overridden per item by a human, because the classifier does not get a veto over a parent's judgement about their own family.

`indeterminate` means nobody knows: no result row, model unavailable or unloadable, load-gate denial, config digest mismatch, inference error or timeout, or evidence that no longer matches. It may NOT be overridden by anything, because 'nobody checked' is not a decision somebody made.

scores.description: Per-class probabilities, when the classifier ran. Null on `indeterminate` -- an indeterminate verdict with scores attached is a contradiction, and the conditional below rejects it.

indeterminate_reason.description: Why nobody knows. Required on `indeterminate`, because 'blocked for an unknown reason' is unactionable and the remedies differ completely: a missing model needs installing, a stale evidence id needs re-running, a digest mismatch needs investigating.

override.description: A human decision to publish despite a `blocked` verdict. Permitted ONLY on `blocked`; the conditional below refuses it on `indeterminate`, which is the single most important rule in this file.

allOf.$comment: An indeterminate verdict must say why, must carry no scores, and must not be overridable. This is the contract-level expression of 'absence blocks': if it were only enforced in code, one caller passing an override would silently reopen the hole.
An override only means anything against a positive result. On a cleared item it would be noise that looks like a decision.
A determinate verdict was produced by a model that returned numbers. Requiring them makes a verdict re-auditable against a changed threshold without re-running inference.

Override.title: Override
Override.description: A recorded human decision. Attributable on purpose: an override that nobody owns is a bypass.

decided_by.description: Local user identifier. Never a service account, never a config value -- a machine cannot consent on a person's behalf about their own photographs.

scope.description: `item_and_sink` is the only value, deliberately. There is no 'always allow this photo' and no 'always allow this class': a decision to print a photo in a private family book is not a decision to publish it, and the whole design fails if an override can outlive the publication it was made for.

ClearanceDecision.title: ClearanceDecision
ClearanceDecision.description: The aggregate, derived from `items` and recomputed by every verifier rather than trusted. It is stored so a rejected publication can be explained without re-running anything -- not so a reader can skip checking the items.

cleared_for_publication.description: True only when EVERY item is `cleared`, or is `blocked` with a valid override for this sink. One indeterminate item denies the whole publication -- a book is printed as a unit and a share is published as a unit, so partial clearance is not a state either can be in.

allOf.$comment: The one arithmetic invariant worth encoding: a publication cannot be cleared while any item is indeterminate. Stated here as well as in prose because this is the rule everything else in the file exists to protect, and a schema that permits the contradiction invites an implementation that produces it.
